title: Apple’s iPhone Duo Strategy: Why a More Expensive iPhone Could Sell More “Cheaper” iPhones
text: Medium Apple’s iPhone Duo Strategy: Why a More Expensive iPhone Could Sell More “Cheaper” iPhones | by Farhad Rezazadeh, PhD, MBA | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Apple IPhone Product Strategy Marketing Strategy Technology Apple’s iPhone Duo Strategy: Why a More Expensive iPhone Could Sell More “Cheaper” iPhones Farhad Rezazadeh, PhD, MBA 4 min read · Sep 25, 2026 -- Listen Share Apple’s introduction of the iPhone Duo is more than the launch of a new smartphone. It is a carefully designed pricing and product-positioning strategy. Press enter or click to view image in full size The iPhone Duo is Apple’s first foldable iPhone. It opens into a 7.6-inch display, offers new multitasking features, and starts at $1,999. By comparison, the iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. All three models use Apple’s A20 Pro chip, but they target different types of customers. The important question is this: Could the expensive iPhone Duo encourage customers to buy the less expensive iPhone Pro or Pro Max? The answer is yes. The iPhone Duo creates a powerful price anchor. Apple is using the iPhone Duo as a premium price anchor. When customers see a $1,999 smartphone, the $1,199 iPhone Pro and $1,299 Pro Max appear more affordable by comparison. These phones are still expensive, but they seem to offer stronger value. This is a psychological pricing strategy. Apple does not need every customer to buy the Duo. Instead, the Duo changes how customers evaluate the rest of the iPhone lineup. A customer who expected to spend around $1,000 may now think: The Duo is too expensive, but the Pro Max is much more reasonable. The iPhone Duo therefore functions as both a product and a reference point for the entire premium iPhone range. 2. Apple separates the products by lifestyle. Apple has designed the three phones for different use cases. The iPhone Duo is aimed at customers who want a large display, multitasking, reading, video, note-taking, and the novelty of a foldable design. Its inner screen is 50 percent larger than the iPhone 18 Pro Max’s display. The iPhone Pro and Pro Max remain stronger choices for photography, videography, battery life, and traditional smartphone use. They offer more advanced camera systems, including a telephoto camera and variable aperture. The Pro Max also offers longer battery life than the Duo in several usage scenarios. This differentiation is important because Apple is not presenting the Duo as a universally superior iPhone. Instead, it is presenting it as a different category of premium device. The message is simple: - Choose Duo for the foldable screen and multitasking. - Choose Pro for photography and portability. - Choose Pro Max for a large traditional display and longer battery life. This reduces direct competition between Apple’s own products. 3. The Duo creates a “halo effect”. The iPhone Duo gives Apple an innovation halo. For several years, smartphone companies have competed with foldable phones. By entering this category, Apple can appear technologically ambitious while keeping its mainstream products familiar and profitable. Even customers who do not buy the Duo may still benefit from its image. The product makes the entire iPhone family look more advanced. It creates attention, media coverage, and consumer curiosity around Apple’s other products. This is similar to how luxury brands use flagship products. The flagship may sell in smaller numbers, but it raises the perceived value of the entire brand. 4. The Pro models become the rational choice. The iPhone Duo’s limitations may actually strengthen the position of the Pro and Pro Max. The Duo costs $700 more than the Pro Max at the same entry point, but the Pro Max has advantages in cameras, Face ID, battery life, and traditional durability. The Duo also replaces Face ID with Touch ID and offers fewer professional photography and video features. For many customers, the Pro Max becomes the rational purchase. A buyer may think: I want the best iPhone, but I do not need a folding screen. The Pro Max gives me better cameras and battery life for less money. That decision still benefits Apple. The customer remains inside Apple’s premium ecosystem and may also purchase AppleCare, accessories, iCloud storage, and other services. 5. Apple is expanding the premium market. The Duo also allows Apple to reach customers who might not have upgraded to a normal iPhone. Some consumers are attracted by a larger screen, tablet-like productivity, or a new form factor. These customers may be willing to pay a premium for something genuinely different. At the same time, customers who dislike the price or do not trust foldable technology can choose the Pro or Pro Max. Apple is therefore expanding its premium market without forcing every customer into the new design. The Duo creates a new ceiling for iPhone prices, while the Pro models remain strong alternatives below that ceiling. 6. The main risk is cannibalization. Apple’s strategy is not without risk. Some customers who would normally buy the Pro Max may choose the Duo instead. If the Duo has lower margins, limited availability, or expensive manufacturing costs, this could reduce Apple’s profitability. There is also a risk that customers will see the Duo as too expensive or unnecessary. Foldable phones still need to prove their long-term durability and usefulness. If customers do not regularly use the large inner screen, the $700 premium may be difficult to justify. For this reason, Apple must continue to give the Pro and Pro Max meaningful advantages. The company needs customers to see them as premium alternatives rather than outdated versions of the Duo. The iPhone Duo may become an important product even if it does not become Apple’s best-selling iPhone.
